title: National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) SR&ED Ruling
subject: FCA appeal by an SR&ED consulting firm over denied software development claims and excluded expert evidence.
summary: National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 confirms SR&ED claimants must satisfy the five-part Northwest Hydraulic test under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The Federal Court of Appeal held CRA guidelines cannot override this test, upheld excluding a largely taxpayer-written expert report, and affirmed denial for lacking contemporaneous, systematic testing records.
metaDescription: Discover key insights from the National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) decision in the Federal Court of Appeal on Canadian SR&ED claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The appellate decision of the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming National Research & Development Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47; application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed with costs, SCC File No. 40303) stands as a watershed authority in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax jurisprudence. Rendered by Justice Donald J. Rennie on May 3, 2022, the ruling solidifies two foundational pillars of Canadian tax law. First, the Court confirmed that the five-part common-law framework established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC) represents the binding statutory interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (ITA), remaining wholly unaffected by administrative rewording in Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) guidelines. Second, the Court affirmed that technical expert reports tendered in the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) will be ruled strictly inadmissible under the doctrine in White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23 if they fail the threshold requirements of impartiality and independence, read as an exercise in advocacy, or offer an opinion on the application of the law to the facts, which fails the requirement of necessity because, with the exception of foreign law, a court does not need an expert opinion on how to apply the law.
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

The appellant, National Research & Development Inc. (National), is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) incorporated on January 1, 2011, operating a specialized consulting practice across engineering, information technology, SR&ED investment tax credits, and Ontario interactive digital media tax credits. A striking feature of this litigation is the deep professional credentialing of National's sole shareholder, president, and primary technical developer, Mr. Amit Saini. Holding a Bachelor of Engineering (McMaster, 2003), a Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) licence (2007), an MBA (Wilfrid Laurier, 2010), and both CMA (2011) and CPA (2012) accounting designations, Mr. Saini had previously served as an SR&ED manager at Meyers Norris Penny and as a senior SR&ED specialist at ATS Automation Tooling Systems.

During its taxation year ended July 31, 2011, National undertook an internal software development initiative known as the "Project Tracking System" (PTS Project), executed directly by Mr. Saini with the assistance of a student employee. The overarching commercial objective of the PTS Project was to build a web-based, cross-platform, and cross-browser software framework capable of tracking claimable SR&ED projects for National's consulting clients and automating certain portions of filing SR&ED claims with the CRA. The architecture required a secure central repository where multiple external clients could input proprietary project records via web browsers while strictly isolating and filtering data visibility so that clients could view only their own specific entries.

To satisfy these security requirements while adhering to internal corporate limitations, National structured the PTS Project around a multi-tiered architecture (MTA) integrating ActiveX Data Objects (ADO), Classic ASP, COM+, and Microsoft SQL Server 2000. Crucially, the development operated under two self-imposed corporate constraints: a strict capital cost constraint dictating that the software use only legacy licences and tools already owned by National, and an expertise constraint limiting the technology stack to languages and frameworks with which National's personnel had existing familiarity.

Within this constrained legacy environment, Phase 1 of the 2011 taxation year focused on three discrete technical sub-objectives. Under Objective 1, National sought to develop algorithms and techniques for record set paging, sorting, and indexing across large datasets compatible with the MTA, subject to a strict maximum system response latency of five seconds. Under Objective 2, the taxpayer aimed to develop a mechanism for in-memory array initialization of joint record sets capable of generating dynamic "pivot-like output" within the legacy SQL Server 2000 environment. Under Objective 3, National attempted to devise methods to enforce deterministic and stateful client-side browser control across disparate web environments. For the 2011 taxation year, National claimed $68,029 in qualifying SR&ED current expenditures and claimed a corresponding federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) of $23,810.
The Minister's Challenge and Procedural History

By Notice of Assessment dated November 3, 2014, the Minister of National Revenue disallowed the entirety of the $68,029 SR&ED expenditure claim and the $23,810 ITC on the basis that the PTS Project activities did not satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. At the TCC hearing, the Crown and the appellant filed a final Joint Statement of Facts stipulating that, should the Court determine that the underlying software engineering activities constituted eligible SR&ED, the quantum of qualified current SR&ED expenditures at issue would be fixed at $42,284.54.

body.text: Governing Statutory Framework

The Canadian SR&ED tax incentive program operates through a bifurcated statutory mechanism under the ITA, providing taxpayers with both special expenditure deductibility rules and an additional investment tax credit (ITC). The statutory gateway to both incentives is the substantive definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". This overarching requirement is categorized into three foundational pillars: paragraph (a) covers basic research undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; paragraph (b) encompasses applied research undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and paragraph (c) governs experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Where foundational work under paragraph (a), (b), or (c) is established, paragraph (d) includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer respecting engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) explicitly exclude work with respect to market research or sales promotion, quality control or routine testing, research in the social sciences or the humanities, prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas, the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, the commercial use of a new or improved process, style changes, and routine data collection.

To operationalize subsection 248(1), Canadian courts apply the five cumulative criteria formulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic (at para. 16). This judicial framework requires the court to determine first whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the inquiry examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the court assesses whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the analysis evaluates whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, the framework asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept as the work progressed.
Final Holding of the Courts

At the Tax Court of Canada, Justice Dominique Lafleur dismissed National's appeal with costs. In a nuanced evidentiary analysis, Justice Lafleur agreed with the taxpayer that genuine technological uncertainty existed (Criterion 1) and that initial hypotheses were formulated (Stages 1 through 4 of Criterion 2), but held that the taxpayer failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that it conducted methodical and systematic testing of those hypotheses, adhered to the scientific method, achieved a technological advancement, or maintained adequate contemporaneous records. Justice Lafleur also refused to qualify National's external consultant, Mr. Dowd, as an expert witness, while accepting Mr. Saini as a "litigant expert" pursuant to Kaul v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 55.

On appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal, National contended that the TCC judge made legal errors in her understanding of subsection 248(1), made palpable and overriding errors in assessing the evidence, misunderstood the burden of proof on the taxpayer (an argument raised for the first time on appeal), and erred by treating the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion (adherence to the scientific method) as a mandatory statutory condition rather than flexible guidance, and by ruling Mr. Dowd's expert report inadmissible. Applying the appellate standard of review—correctness for questions of law and palpable and overriding error for questions of fact or mixed fact and law—Justice Rennie (Woods and Laskin JJ.A. concurring) dismissed the appeal with costs. The FCA held that the Northwest Hydraulic test is the authoritative legal construction of subsection 248(1) as settled in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, that CRA administrative guidelines cannot override judicial statutory interpretation, and that the TCC properly excluded a partial, taxpayer-authored expert report.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of National's claim in National R&D Inc. v. Canada offers an exceptional diagnostic study for Canadian tax practitioners because the taxpayer did not lose at the initial threshold of technological uncertainty. Instead, the claim collapsed across the operational, methodological, and evidentiary dimensions of the SR&ED regime. A granular examination of these failures reveals how technical execution, corporate record-keeping, and litigation strategy intersect in Canadian tax disputes.
The Nuance of Criterion 1: How Business and Economic Constraints Frame Technological Uncertainty

Before dissecting the taxpayer's operational failures, it is essential to examine why National prevailed on the first Northwest Hydraulic criterion at the TCC, as this aspect of the ruling carries significant doctrinal weight for Canadian applied science claims. At trial, the Minister assumed that no technological uncertainties existed in any of National's objectives and that the PTS Project could be carried out using well-known IT techniques. Specifically regarding Objective 2 (generating pivot-like output from joint record sets in memory), the Crown argued that Microsoft SQL Server 2005 contained a built-in PIVOT command that represented a standard method used by competent IT professionals in 2011.

Justice Lafleur rejected the Crown's position, establishing a vital principle (subsequently examined in 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17) that economic considerations, business constraints, and the specific business context of the taxpayer claiming the SR&ED credit are relevant factors when evaluating technological uncertainty. Relying on paragraph 2.10.2 of CRA Information Circular 86-4R3, Justice Lafleur explained that technological uncertainty arises either when it is uncertain whether the goals can be achieved at all, or when a taxpayer is uncertain which alternative routes, system architectures, or configurations will work or meet desired cost and specification targets. Because National operated within a mandatory MTA framework and was restricted by corporate cost constraints to SQL Server 2000 during the 2011 taxation year, the existence of the PIVOT command in SQL Server 2005 was legally irrelevant. Furthermore, it was not established on the evidence that PIVOT would have achieved National's objectives or been compatible with the MTA, rendering the resolution of the uncertainties not reasonably predictable. On appeal, the FCA rejected the contention that Justice Lafleur had adopted a restrictive approach to the scientific method, finding no indication that her understanding of subsection 248(1) was unsuitable for the applied sciences and noting that she had acknowledged the criteria must be applied within the context of National's business environment.

However, prevailing on technological uncertainty created a strategic vulnerability for the appellant. Establishing that an objective cannot be resolved through standard procedures within a constrained architecture merely satisfies the threshold gateway of subsection 248(1); it does not relieve the taxpayer of the affirmative statutory burden to execute and prove a methodical, systematic investigation to resolve that uncertainty.
Statutory Misinterpretation and the Fallacy of Administrative Reliance

Facing profound evidentiary deficits regarding how its software testing was actually executed, National advanced an ambitious statutory interpretation argument before the FCA. The appellant argued that Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic—which asks whether the procedure adopted accorded with the "total discipline of the scientific method"—lacks any textual foundation in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and should be treated as mere guidance rather than a mandatory legal prerequisite. To bolster this position, National pointed to the CRA's updated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, released on August 13, 2021. Because the 2021 CRA Guidelines replaced the archived policy and omitted explicit references to the "five questions" and the "scientific method" in favour of plainer English, National contended that the tax authority had eliminated the requirement to follow the scientific method.

Justice Rennie held that this argument failed for several reasons. First, Justice Rennie relied on the FCA's prior holding in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, in which the Court rejected a similar argument and affirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the appropriate interpretation of subsection 248(1), and he further held that National's argument misunderstood the relationship between the courts and legislation, because Parliament and the legislatures rely on the courts to give definition, amplitude and precision to statutory language. Guided by the rules of statutory interpretation, the courts have determined that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the appropriate legal construction of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) and reflect the judiciary's understanding of what Parliament intended. Second, regarding the status of administrative guidance, the Court confirmed that, while CRA guidance is useful context in understanding the purpose and intent of a particular provision, it is not binding on the courts, which are guided instead by the rules of statutory interpretation set out in Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54, and by precedent. Third, addressing the substantive content of the 2021 CRA Guidelines, the FCA disagreed that the revised guidance rejected the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, observing that while the new CRA guidance no longer uses the precise language of the "scientific method," its "The 'How' requirement" section still speaks to the requirement of an underlying rigour or discipline in the experimental process. The 2021 guidelines explicitly require the generation of a hypothesis consistent with known facts, the testing of that hypothesis by experiment or analysis, the development of logical conclusions based on those findings, and the keeping of evidence generated as the work progresses—which mirrors the exact underlying discipline of the scientific method and the original Northwest Hydraulic framework.
Failure to Execute and Prove Methodical Hypothesis Testing (Criteria 2, 3, and 4)

The core substantive failure in National R&D Inc. occurred at the operational transition from hypothesis formulation to empirical verification. Under Northwest Hydraulic (at para. 16), Justice Bowman articulated a five-stage process governing the second criterion: the observation of the subject matter of the problem; the formulation of a clear objective; the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypothesis or hypotheses.

While Mr. Saini's testimony, a letter dated May 12, 2012 to the CRA, and a Project Timeline convinced Justice Lafleur on a balance of probabilities that initial hypotheses were formulated for each of the three PTS Project objectives, the second criterion was ultimately not met because it requires the methodical and systematic testing of those hypotheses. As subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence applying National R&D emphasizes (such as Justice Spiro's ruling in Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen, 2022 TCC 62), Justice Bowman deliberately utilized the plural "hypotheses" throughout the second, third, and fifth criteria. The legal standard does not contemplate a single, overarching project conjecture; rather, it mandates a discrete hypothesis that precedes each specific test and is systematically modified in light of the empirical results of that test.

In National R&D, the taxpayer failed to demonstrate that it conducted its software development in a methodical manner. Neither the documentary record nor Mr. Saini's oral testimony provided specifics regarding the testing methodologies deployed, the exact number of tests conducted for Objectives 2 and 3, the controlled variations between individual tests, or specific measurable results. Without evidence reflecting a logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests, the Court could not conclude that National carried out a systematic investigation in respect of the PTS Project. Because National failed to prove that a systematic investigation was carried out in accordance with the scientific method, it likewise failed Criterion 4: although Justice Lafleur accepted Mr. Saini's testimony that some technological advancement occurred, she held that it was not an advancement within the meaning of the SR&ED definition, because a qualifying advancement requires that technological uncertainties be removed through a process of systematic investigation.
Contemporaneous Documentation Deficiencies and Post-Hoc Reconstruction (Criterion 5)

Although Justice Lafleur noted at paragraph 66 of the TCC decision (citing Formadrain Inc.) that the ITA does not strictly mandate documentary evidence to the exclusion of oral testimony, the Court cautioned that there are risks associated with not adequately documenting a step in an SR&ED project. In National R&D, Mr. Saini's testimony was far too vague to overcome the absence of contemporaneous records, and every category of documentary evidence submitted by the appellant suffered from fatal flaws.

The most damaging evidentiary failure involved a table tendered by the appellant titled "Trials to Achieve Sorting & Paging With Set Constraints", which purported to outline 50 experiments conducted for Objective 1. Upon judicial scrutiny, the table proved unhelpful because multiple experiments were grouped together indiscriminately, the testing methods were unclear, and the recorded results were vague without showing how any outcome modified a subsequent hypothesis. Crucially, under cross-examination, Mr. Saini admitted that this 50-experiment table was created after the fact specifically for the CRA audit, and National failed to submit the underlying contemporaneous basic version into evidence. For Objectives 2 and 3, no similar experimental tables existed at all. As a result, Justice Lafleur did not find the after-the-fact table very helpful and could not treat it, or any other document tendered by National, as contemporaneous documentation detailing the tests conducted and their results.

Similarly, National attempted to substantiate its software development by introducing fragments of computer source code. However, the appellant submitted only isolated code snapshots and failed to adduce source code revision histories or multiple sequential code versions. As Justice Lafleur observed at paragraph 57, a court cannot deduce an experimental trend or code advancement from "a single data point". Without version histories demonstrating how the code evolved across failed and modified tests, isolated code fragments cannot establish adherence to the scientific method. Finally, the Project Timeline and task documents submitted by National merely listed tasks and dates without recording the formulation, testing, or modification of hypotheses or demonstrating any logical progression between entries.
Expert Witness Disqualification: The White Burgess Trap

A major focal point of the FCA decision in National R&D Inc. is the affirmance of the TCC's refusal to admit the expert report of Mr. Dowd, an external expert hired by National for the appeal. Under Canadian evidentiary law, the admissibility of expert opinion evidence is governed by the two-step gatekeeping framework established by the Supreme Court of Canada in White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23 (adopting R. v. Mohan, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 9 and R. v. Abbey, 2009 ONCA 624), which requires that expert opinion evidence first meet the threshold requirements of relevance, necessity, the absence of an exclusionary rule, and a properly qualified expert (including impartiality and independence), and then survive a second, discretionary gatekeeping step in which the trial judge decides whether the evidence is sufficiently beneficial to the trial process to warrant its admission despite its potential harm; the procedural requirements for expert reports are governed separately by section 145 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure). Evidence failing to meet this threshold is strictly inadmissible.

The TCC found that Mr. Dowd's report did not comply with section 145(2) of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) or paragraphs 3(d), (e), (g) and (h) of the Code of Conduct for Expert Witnesses, as it did not set out the proposed evidence in full, did not identify the source of the facts and assumptions, and did not include the source material; on substance, both the TCC and the FCA found the report inadmissible due to three converging defects. First, the proposed expert lacked impartiality and independence because National itself had written 65% of the expert report. Second, in tone and substance, the report functioned as "an exercise in advocacy" on behalf of the litigant rather than an objective technical analysis. Third, because the report was an opinion on the application of the law to the facts, it failed the requirement of necessity; as the FCA put it, with the exception of foreign law, a court does not need an expert opinion on how to apply the law. The TCC further held that the report failed at the second, discretionary gatekeeping stage, and the FCA saw no error in that conclusion. While the Tax Court has recognized that applied-science work such as computer software, algorithms and databases can constitute SR&ED (as in Allegro Wireless Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 27), the FCA confirmed in National R&D (and as subsequently cited in Canafric and BlackBerry Limited v. The King, 2023 TCC 137) that, because there are no bright lines in this gatekeeping exercise, a trial judge's decision not to admit expert evidence will not be reversed on appeal absent an error in principle, a material misapprehension of the evidence, or an unreasonable conclusion.

On appeal, National alleged that without the benefit of Mr. Dowd's expert report, Justice Lafleur did not understand the technical software evidence and was unable to assess whether it conformed to subsection 248(1). Justice Rennie firmly rejected this contention, writing that the trial judge's reasons demonstrated a careful regard to the evidence. Moreover, the TCC had already qualified Mr. Saini as a "litigant expert" (following Kaul v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 55), enabling him to testify directly regarding the technical aspects of the PTS Project. The claim failed not from any judicial inability to comprehend software architecture, but because the appellant did not conduct its work methodically and failed to keep adequate, logically progressive records.

Standard: Gatekeeping threshold requiring necessity, impartiality, independence, and non-usurpation of the ultimate legal issue. Holding (Excluded / Inadmissible): 65% of the report was written by the appellant; it did not comply with s. 145(2) of the Tax Court Rules or the Code of Conduct for Expert Witnesses; it constituted an "exercise in advocacy," and, as an opinion on the application of s. 248(1) to the facts, failed the necessity requirement and the second gatekeeping stage.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate holdings of National R&D Inc. v. Canada into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian corporate taxpayers, two comprehensive industry case studies are presented below. Each case study models a realistic Canadian enterprise confronting the exact legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls exposed by Justice Lafleur and Justice Rennie, followed by a step-by-step remedial restructuring blueprint.
Case Study 1: Enterprise FinTech Software & Legacy Architecture Integration
Industry Scenario and Project Background

Valoris FinTech Solutions Inc. ("Valoris") is a Toronto-based CCPC providing real-time regulatory compliance and anti-money laundering (AML) transaction monitoring software to Canadian credit unions. Valoris operates a legacy core transaction engine built on a multi-tiered architecture utilizing .NET Framework 4.8 and an on-premise relational database (Microsoft SQL Server 2014). Due to strict multi-year data residency and regulatory audit-lock agreements with its credit union clients, Valoris is contractually and economically prohibited from migrating its clients to cloud-native graph databases or upgrading the underlying database engine. Within these rigid architectural and capital constraints, Valoris launches the "Velocity-AML Project" during its 2026 taxation year to achieve two technical objectives: first, developing a deterministic in-memory graph-traversal and entity-resolution caching mechanism within the legacy relational architecture capable of joining and scoring 10 million cross-institutional transaction records with a maximum p99 response latency under 250 milliseconds; and second, devising a custom lock-free concurrency control protocol to prevent thread starvation during simultaneous high-frequency read/write ingestion without triggering SQL Server 2014 tempdb contention.
Identification of National R&D Pitfalls

As initially executed by Valoris's engineering team, the Velocity-AML Project is headed toward complete disallowance under National R&D Inc. v. Canada due to three systemic vulnerabilities. First, the engineering team falls into the "single data point" source code trap: developers routinely overwrite broken experimental branches and commit only the final, working production code to the main repository at the end of each two-week Agile sprint, leaving behind no version history of failed algorithms or intermediate code states. Second, the company falls into the retrospective audit table trap: nine months after fiscal year-end, an external SR&ED consultant interviews the lead architect and compiles an after-the-fact summary spreadsheet listing "40 Optimization Trials" with generic outcomes ("Too slow," "Memory leak," "Success") to respond to a CRA Request for Information, without retaining any underlying raw benchmark logs. Third, in its draft Form T661 narrative, Valoris mischaracterizes its business constraints by focusing heavily on commercial budget limitations rather than articulating how the fixed legacy SQL Server 2014 memory manager creates an objective system-level technological uncertainty.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Framing Technological Uncertainty Within Architectural Constraints (Criterion 1)

To replicate National's success on Criterion 1 while insulating the claim from a "routine engineering" or "purely economic obstacle" challenge under 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, Valoris must establish an objective technical baseline prior to initiating experimental coding. The Lead Architect must author a dated Pre-Project Architecture and Baseline Limitation Memo that documents the exact commercial and regulatory constraints locking the multi-tiered system into .NET 4.8 and SQL Server 2014. Crucially, this memo must demonstrate why standard procedures available to a competent database professional—such as standard B-tree composite indexing, native SQL Server 2014 In-Memory OLTP (Hekaton), or standard JOIN hints—cannot resolve the uncertainty. By recording initial baseline benchmark tests showing that native Hekaton tables fail due to fixed memory-optimized table size ceilings under Valoris's hardware footprint (resulting in a baseline latency of 4,200 ms against the 250 ms specification), Valoris successfully translates an economic constraint into a genuine system-level technological uncertainty under paragraph 2.10.2 of IC 86-4R3.
Step 2: Implementing Automated Contemporaneous Code & Experiment Provenance (Criteria 2, 3, and 5)

To eliminate the "isolated code snapshot" failure identified by Justice Lafleur at paragraph 70 of 2020 TCC 47, Valoris must restructure its Git version control and Jira ticketing workflows to enforce contemporaneous, immutable provenance. Engineering governance policies must strictly prohibit squashing or deleting failed experimental Git branches; instead, every experimental iteration must be committed to a dedicated branch following a standardized naming convention such as sred/exp-[Objective#]-[Hypothesis#] (for example, sred/exp-01-H03). Furthermore, automated Git commit hooks must enforce a structured commit template requiring developers to log four mandatory fields at the exact timestamp of each test commit: the specific discrete hypothesis tested, the architectural variable modified, the empirical benchmark result (latency and memory consumption), and a causal analysis of why the failure occurred alongside the resulting modification to the next hypothesis. Finally, every experimental build in the continuous integration (CI/CD) pipeline must trigger an automated load-testing harness that outputs a timestamped JSON telemetry log linked directly to the Git commit SHA hash, ensuring that every assertion in the T661 narrative traces directly to a dated, contemporaneous artifact.

body.text: Step 3: Restructuring Subcontractor and Employee Governance Contracts

To ensure that all supporting computer programming, data collection, and testing activities qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d) and survive CRA financial audit verification, Valoris must align its human resource and procurement contracts with statutory boundaries. In National R&D, Mr. Saini conducted the project alongside a student assistant. Valoris must implement daily time-tracking integrated directly with Jira ticket IDs so that student or junior developer hours spent executing test harnesses on sred/exp-* branches are rigorously segregated from routine user-interface coding or commercial production deployment excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i). Furthermore, where Valoris engages Canadian third-party software contractors, the Master Services Agreement (MSA) and Statement of Work (SOW) must explicitly stipulate that all supporting work is performed physically within Canada on behalf of Valoris, that all intellectual property, source code revision histories, and failed experimental test logs vest immediately in Valoris, and that contractor invoices are itemized by specific experimental Jira ticket and Git branch rather than commercial deliverables.
Case Study 2: Advanced Industrial Manufacturing & Embedded Control Systems
Industry Scenario and Project Background

Borealis Precision Hydraulics Corp. ("Borealis") is an Ontario-based CCPC that designs and manufactures heavy-duty electro-hydraulic actuation systems for cold-climate mining equipment. During its 2026 taxation year, Borealis initiates the "Arctic-Valve Project" to develop a closed-loop proportional solenoid valve controller and novel elastomeric seal geometry capable of maintaining micro-positioning accuracy (±10 µm) across extreme thermal transients (−50 °C to +80 °C) without fluid cavitation or seal extrusion. The project is directed by Borealis's Vice President of Engineering (a licensed P.Eng.), who simultaneously serves as the corporation's internal SR&ED claim coordinator.
Identification of National R&D Pitfalls

Borealis's project execution and subsequent litigation posture exhibit three critical legal vulnerabilities directly mirroring National R&D Inc. v. Canada and Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen. First, Borealis relies on a single overarching project conjecture—postulating generally that modifying the valve spool geometry and tuning the PID controller will allow the actuator to operate accurately at −50 °C—while shop-floor technicians physically swap seals and tweak PID gains via unstructured trial-and-error without formulating discrete hypotheses prior to each bench test. Second, shop-floor documentation consists merely of pass/fail checkmarks written on a whiteboard, which the VP of Engineering summarizes months after year-end into a high-level T661 narrative lacking test methodologies, variable progressions, or quantitative failure analyses. Third, upon receiving a CRA Notice of Confirmation disallowing the claim, Borealis retains an external mechanical engineering consultant to submit an Expert Report to the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure, but to reduce legal costs, Borealis's VP of Engineering drafts 80% of the report himself and instructs the external consultant to conclude that Borealis's work satisfied the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and constituted eligible SR&ED under subsection 248(1).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Replacing Shop-Floor Trial-and-Error with the Five-Stage Scientific Discipline (Criteria 2, 3, and 4)

To satisfy Justice Bowman's five-stage hypothesis process as strictly enforced in National R&D Inc. (2020 TCC 47 at para. 45; 2022 FCA 72) and Dave's Diesel (2022 TCC 62), Borealis must replace ad-hoc shop-floor tweaking with a mandatory Engineering Design of Experiments (DoE) Protocol. Prior to placing any prototype valve assembly into the environmental cold chamber, the supervising P.Eng. must issue a sequentially numbered Experimental Test Traveller attached directly to the shop work order. Each Test Traveller must articulate a discrete, predictive physical hypothesis linking a controlled independent variable—such as PTFE-fluorosilicone co-polymer Shore D hardness or pulse-width modulation dithering frequency—to a measurable dependent physical parameter, such as breakaway stiction force in Newtons at −50 °C. Immediately following each cold-chamber cycle, raw oscilloscope pressure traces and laser displacement sensor logs must be exported with immutable timestamps and appended to the Test Traveller, accompanied by a contemporaneous engineering analysis explaining which specific requirement was not met (per the winning template noted in Canafric, 2023 TCC 108) and how that empirical finding dictates the modified hypothesis for the subsequent prototype iteration.
Step 2: Structuring Commercial Customer Contracts to Prevent Commercial Production Exclusions

Where Borealis develops custom hydraulic actuators intended for ultimate supply to mining original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), contractual ambiguity can disqualify the claim as commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i) or reduce qualified expenditures through contract payment exclusions. Borealis must restructure its OEM commercial agreements to establish a strict legal and financial demarcation between the pre-commercial Experimental Prototype Development Phase and subsequent commercial production. The contract terms must explicitly stipulate that Borealis retains full technical risk and sole ownership of all foreground hydraulic control intellectual property, and that customer milestone payments are contingent strictly upon the delivery of commercial production units meeting standard acceptance specifications rather than reimbursing Borealis for experimental engineering hours. Furthermore, physical valve prototypes destroyed or rendered unusable during cold-chamber destructive testing must be recorded in a contemporaneous Scrap and Destructive Testing Ledger with serial numbers and photographic documentation, proving that the materials were consumed directly in experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) rather than commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i).
Step 3: Litigation-Ready Expert Witness Governance under White Burgess

To avoid the catastrophic exclusion of expert evidence suffered by the appellant in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, Borealis and its tax litigation counsel must enforce a rigorous evidentiary firewall when retaining an independent expert witness for the Tax Court of Canada under the White Burgess framework. The table below contrasts the fatal evidentiary errors committed in National R&D against the mandatory remedial protocol required to satisfy the Tax Court's gatekeeping threshold:

headers: Fatal Practice in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72)
Remedial Best-Practice Protocol for Canadian Tax Litigation

cells: Authorship & Independence
The appellant (National) wrote 65% of the expert report signed by Mr. Dowd, destroying threshold independence under White Burgess.

Strict Firewall on Drafting: The independent expert must research and write 100% of the report independently. Tax counsel may review draft reports solely to ensure clarity, responsiveness to the mandate questions, and procedural compliance, never to insert technical arguments, and the taxpayer's employees must never draft a single sentence of the report.
Tone & Impartiality
The report read as "an exercise in advocacy" arguing the taxpayer's case rather than providing an objective technical assessment.

Objective Duty to the Court: The expert must execute the mandatory Certificate Concerning Code of Conduct for Expert Witnesses, explicitly acknowledging a paramount duty to assist the Tax Court impartially, and must candidly identify any tests or sub-activities where documentation is incomplete.
Framing of Mandate Questions (The "Ultimate Issue" Rule)

The expert opined directly on the application of subsection 248(1) of the ITA to the facts, which failed the requirement of necessity because, with the exception of foreign law, a court does not need an expert opinion on how to apply the law.

Strictly Technical Mandate Questions: Counsel's letter of instruction must never ask the expert whether the work constitutes "SR&ED" or satisfies Northwest Hydraulic. Instead, counsel must pose purely technical questions: (1) What was the state of the art and standard engineering practice in electro-hydraulic seal design at −50 °C in 2026? (2) Could a competent hydraulic engineer resolve the thermal stiction problem using published engineering handbooks or off-the-shelf components? (3) Do the dated oscilloscope logs and Test Travellers reflect a methodical, hypothesis-driven engineering investigation?
Role of the "Litigant Expert" vs. Independent Expert
National relied on Mr. Saini as a "litigant expert" (Kaul, 2017 TCC 55), whose oral testimony remained too vague to overcome missing contemporaneous test logs.

Complementary Evidentiary Division: The internal VP of Engineering testifies strictly as a participant / litigant expert to authenticate the contemporaneous Test Travellers, explain the chronological sequence of tests, and detail the business constraints. The external independent expert testifies solely to establish the objective industry baseline and validate that the recorded test parameters represent non-routine engineering.

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis & Jurisprudential Conclusions

The Federal Court of Appeal's decision in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72—reinforced by the Supreme Court of Canada's refusal to grant leave to appeal in March 2023—cements a rigorous, unforgiving evidentiary paradigm for Canadian SR&ED claimants. Viewed alongside Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, the ruling extinguishes any lingering expectation among taxpayers that administrative simplifications in CRA web publications or plain-language filing guides will relax the substantive legal threshold enforced by the Canadian judiciary.

Three overarching strategic conclusions emerge from this jurisprudence for Canadian tax counsel, corporate executives, and technical R&D leaders. First, the academic or professional credentials of the claimant cannot substitute for contemporaneous experimental records. In National R&D, the taxpayer's sole principal was a licensed Professional Engineer, a Chartered Professional Accountant, and a seasoned SR&ED consultant who successfully convinced the Tax Court that genuine technological uncertainty existed within his company's constrained software architecture. Yet his claim failed completely because he attempted to prove systematic investigation through an after-the-fact audit summary table and isolated snapshots of finished source code. Canadian courts evaluate how the work was systematically conducted and recorded in real time, not the credentials of the witness asserting that it occurred.

Second, business and economic constraints operate as a double-edged sword that must be documented with technical precision. While National R&D confirms that corporate cost limitations and legacy system architectures are legitimate contextual factors in establishing technological uncertainty under Criterion 1, those constraints must be translated into specific system-level technical incompatibilities. Once that uncertainty is framed, the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving that every subsequent step followed the total discipline of the scientific method: formulating a discrete hypothesis prior to each test, systematically measuring variables, analyzing why an iteration failed, and modifying the hypothesis for the next experiment.

Third, litigation readiness begins during the taxation year, and expert witness evidence must be strictly insulated from client advocacy. When an audit dispute escalates to the Tax Court of Canada, no independent expert report can retroactively cure missing experimental progression, and any attempt by a taxpayer to ghostwrite or steer an expert report toward legal conclusions under subsection 248(1) will result in immediate exclusion under White Burgess. Only by embedding automated version provenance, structured hypothesis logs, and disciplined experimental telemetry directly into daily engineering workflows can Canadian corporations reliably defend their SR&ED investment tax credits before the CRA and the federal courts.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; FCA reaffirmed the Northwest Hydraulic test and held CRA administrative guidelines do not displace it.
